body:
What makes a local disaster-management plan usable?

A community disaster-management plan should identify foreseeable local hazards, people who may need assistance, available resources, responsible persons and practical actions before and during an emergency. A written document is useful only when the people expected to follow it understand their responsibilities.

For a village or urban ward, the plan should normally address warning arrangements, safe evacuation routes, assistance for people with additional needs, designated shelters, essential contacts, basic supplies and communication with district authorities. It must also indicate who will update contact details and review arrangements after drills or changes in local conditions.

Local preparedness plans are connected to government institutions. In Gujarat, the Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA) identifies a working structure involving state, district, taluka and village levels. The particular tasks performed at each level depend on applicable law, official plans and administrative arrangements.

LevelInstitution or arrangementBasic responsibility
StateGSDMA and state departmentsState-level planning, guidance, coordination and support
DistrictDistrict Disaster Management AuthorityDistrict planning, coordination and mobilisation of response resources
TalukaTaluka disaster-management arrangementsCoordination between district authorities and local communities
VillageGram Panchayat and village disaster-management arrangementsLocal risk identification, preparedness, participation and reporting

The District Collector chairs the District Disaster Management Authority. In Gujarat's described village-level framework, the Sarpanch chairs the Village Disaster Management Committee. These roles should not be confused with the command structure used to manage a particular incident.

GSDMA was constituted on 8 February 2001 following the destructive Gujarat earthquake of 26 January 2001. Its subsequent activities have included reconstruction, preparedness and disaster-risk reduction. The Gujarat experience illustrates why recovery lessons must inform later local planning.

From an official warning to protective action

An early warning is effective when reliable hazard information reaches the people at risk in time for appropriate action. Issuing a warning is therefore only one part of the process. The message must be received, understood, trusted and connected to a practical action.

District and local authorities may communicate warnings through several channels, including public announcements, telecommunications, local institutions and trained volunteers. Combining methods helps reach people who have limited internet access, cannot read a message or require communication in another language or accessible format.

Last-mile communication is the final part of warning delivery: reaching the intended individual or household rather than merely transmitting a message to an office or a general audience. A warning volunteer should report households that could not be contacted or situations in which the advised action cannot be followed safely.

Warning is not the same as evacuation. A warning communicates danger and appropriate precautions; evacuation is the temporary movement of people to safer places when indicated by the situation and competent authorities.

Choosing and preparing relief shelters

A designated shelter is a place identified for temporary protection or accommodation during an emergency. Depending on local conditions, a suitable school, community centre or purpose-built cyclone shelter may be used. However, a familiar public building does not automatically qualify as a safe shelter.

Authorities need to consider its location relative to the hazard, accessibility, capacity, drinking water, sanitation, lighting, health needs and arrangements for managing occupants. Where necessary, transport must be planned for residents who cannot reach the site independently.

Shelters should support privacy and protection, including arrangements suitable for women, children, older people and persons with disabilities. Shelter preparation also requires communication about who manages the site and how shortages or safety concerns will be reported.

Local planning under the current legal framework

The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025, which came into force on 9 April 2025, strengthened several planning responsibilities. It added a disaster-management planning duty to Section 41 for local authorities. It also inserted Section 41A, enabling a State Government, by notification, to constitute an Urban Disaster Management Authority for its state capital and cities having municipal corporations, excluding the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union territory of Chandigarh.

This is an enabling provision: the words may, by notification do not mean that a separate Urban Disaster Management Authority automatically exists in every eligible city.

Prelims focus

  • GSDMA was constituted on 8 February 2001 after the Gujarat earthquake of 26 January 2001.
  • The District Collector chairs the District Disaster Management Authority.
  • Gujarat's village disaster-management framework identifies the Sarpanch as chair of the Village Disaster Management Committee.
  • Last-mile warning means reaching and enabling action by people at risk.
  • The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 came into force on 9 April 2025.
  • Trap: Section 41A permits notified Urban Disaster Management Authorities; it does not automatically establish one in every eligible city.

[Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Chapter XIII, Sections 13.1, 13.3 and 13.8, institutional framework, emergency-response infrastructure and disaster-management plans; National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction, October 2024, Sections 3.3, 4.2 and 7.1–7.2; Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025, Sections 22–23, amendments to Sections 41 and 41A of the principal Act; Ministry of Home Affairs, parliamentary response on the Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 22 July 2025, commencement date. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Local Disaster Plans, Early Warnings and Safe Shelters

body:
Why a common incident-response structure is necessary

When a major disaster occurs, fire services, police, health workers, district administration, specialised response teams, local bodies and volunteers may all be involved. Without a common structure, different teams could receive conflicting instructions, essential supplies could be sent to the wrong place and urgent requests could go unanswered.

The Incident Response System (IRS) is an organised framework for managing an emergency through defined responsibilities, a clear command structure, common objectives, coordinated resources and systematic communication.

India's IRS draws on the principles of the Incident Command System while adapting them to the country's administrative arrangements. The National Disaster Management Authority issued its Incident Response System guidelines in July 2010. The structure is scalable: a small incident need not activate every position, whereas a major incident may require additional teams and supporting functions.

Responsible Officer and Incident Commander

The Indian IRS distinguishes the Responsible Officer (RO) from the Incident Commander (IC).

At the state level, the Chief Secretary is the Responsible Officer. At the district level, the District Magistrate or District Collector is the Responsible Officer. The RO has overall responsibility for emergency response at the relevant administrative level and arranges the response organisation and resources.

The Incident Commander manages the response to a particular incident through the Incident Response Team. The IC directs the incident-level work within the authority and responsibilities assigned through the response arrangement. Therefore, overall administrative responsibility and direct management of field operations are related but different roles.

Command Staff and General Staff

The Command Staff assist the Incident Commander with matters directly related to command. The General Staff manage major functional sections of the incident response.

IRS role or sectionMain function
Information and Media OfficerCoordinates approved incident information and media communication
Safety OfficerAdvises on risks affecting responders and incident activities
Liaison OfficerFacilitates coordination with participating agencies and organisations
Operations SectionDirects incident-level operational activities, including organised rescue and evacuation work
Planning SectionCollects and assesses situation information and supports preparation of incident action plans
Logistics SectionArranges facilities, services and material support needed for operations

The Incident Action Plan expresses the objectives and planned activities for managing an incident. The Planning Section helps prepare and maintain it, while the Operations Section carries out the assigned operational work. Logistics supports the work by making necessary resources and services available.

In the Indian IRS guidelines, Operations, Planning and Logistics are the 3 principal General Staff sections. The Finance Branch is placed under the Logistics Section. This structure should not be confused with versions of incident-command arrangements used in other countries.

Emergency Operations Centre versus Incident Command Post

An Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) is a coordination and information-support facility. It helps the Responsible Officer maintain an overview of the emergency, communicate with departments, obtain situation reports and organise additional resources.

An Incident Command Post (ICP) is the location from which the Incident Commander performs the primary command functions for a particular incident. Thus, an EOC may support several incident-level activities without becoming the physical command post for each one.

Unified Command

Some emergencies involve several agencies or jurisdictions with overlapping responsibilities. Unified Command enables the participating authorities to establish common incident objectives and strategies while retaining their respective legal responsibilities.

It is not an arrangement in which every agency independently issues competing operational orders. The purpose is coordinated decision-making and an integrated response.

Prelims focus

  • NDMA issued the Indian Incident Response System guidelines in July 2010.
  • At state level, the Chief Secretary is the IRS Responsible Officer; at district level, the District Magistrate or District Collector is the RO.
  • The Incident Commander manages an incident through the Incident Response Team.
  • Command Staff include Information and Media, Safety and Liaison Officers.
  • The 3 principal General Staff sections are Operations, Planning and Logistics.
  • Trap: The EOC supports coordination; it is not automatically the same as the field Incident Command Post.

[National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Incident Response System, July 2010, Section 2.3, IRS principles; Sections 3.4–3.7, state and district coordination and Unified Command; Sections 3.13–3.15, Emergency Operations Centre and Incident Response Team; Chapters 4–8, command and General Staff functions. Guidelines consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Emergency responders need clear responsibilities and coordinated information.

title: Incident Response System: Command, Coordination and Emergency Operations

body:
Coordination means working towards common objectives

Disaster response often requires assistance from several departments and organisations. Coordination ensures that their work contributes to agreed priorities rather than producing overlapping efforts or leaving important needs unattended.

For example, police may regulate access to a dangerous area, health services may arrange medical assistance, public works or utility agencies may report damaged essential services, and trained response teams may perform authorised rescue activities. Community volunteers may help relay information about households requiring support. Each participant has a different function, but all must work within the established response arrangement.

Operations, Planning and Logistics perform different tasks

The Indian Incident Response System groups major functions under Operations, Planning and Logistics. These sections are interdependent, but their responsibilities should not be confused.

  • Operations carries out assigned field activities. Examples include directing organised evacuation work and other incident-level operational tasks.
  • Planning maintains an understanding of the changing situation, records available information and supports the Incident Action Plan.
  • Logistics arranges the services, facilities and supplies required for response activities, including communication support, transport and other operational requirements.

A report that a road is blocked is information for situation assessment. Deciding which field team should undertake an authorised task concerns operations. Arranging a suitable vehicle or equipment for that team concerns logistics. Effective coordination connects these functions.

The role of communication

Operational communication enables responders and authorities to exchange instructions, resource requests, confirmed facts and situation updates. Messages should identify the place concerned, the problem, the assistance required and the responsible contact wherever the situation allows.

Communication must also distinguish verified information from unconfirmed reports. An unverified message circulating on social media can cause confusion, especially when it gives a false evacuation route or incorrect shelter location. Authorities and community volunteers should use confirmed information and correct errors through trusted channels.

Preparedness plans should identify alternative communication methods because electricity, mobile networks or internet connections may fail during an emergency. A backup method might involve an available radio system, another functioning network or an agreed physical reporting arrangement. Its suitability depends on local circumstances.

Logistics and resource accountability

Logistics means ensuring that the right resources reach the required location when they are needed. It involves more than collecting donations or dispatching supplies. Responders need to know what is available, where it is stored, whether a route is usable, who will receive the consignment and whether the request has been fulfilled.

If 2 shelters each request drinking water, a response arrangement should identify their actual needs, existing supplies and delivery constraints. Sending all available water to the first shelter without checking the second may produce unequal and inefficient relief.

Records of resources requested, allocated, dispatched and received help prevent both duplication and shortages. They also support accountability for public resources and donated materials.

Mutual aid extends available capacity

Mutual aid is assistance provided by one jurisdiction, department or organisation to another when the receiving authority requires additional personnel, equipment, supplies or other capabilities.

Mutual aid may involve neighbouring districts, local bodies, specialised services, voluntary organisations or other agencies. Advance arrangements improve response because the parties can identify whom to contact and how resources will be requested and coordinated before an emergency occurs.

Mutual aid should strengthen the established response system. It does not automatically remove the legal responsibilities of the authority requesting assistance or permit supporting organisations to act without coordination.

Why this matters in Gujarat

Gujarat's state and district emergency operations arrangements support communication across administrative levels. During a major coastal or inland emergency, affected districts may require additional transport, medical assistance, shelters or specialist teams. Coordination through the appropriate authorities helps match such assistance to confirmed needs.

Prelims focus

  • Operations directs field activities; Planning maintains situation information and supports the Incident Action Plan.
  • Logistics provides the supplies, facilities and services required for response.
  • The EOC supports information exchange and resource coordination.
  • Verified warnings and incident information should be distinguished from rumours.
  • Mutual aid means organised assistance between jurisdictions or organisations when additional capacity is needed.
  • Trap: Dispatching supplies is not proof of successful delivery; receipt and unmet needs must also be checked.

[National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Incident Response System, July 2010, Sections 2.3.10–2.3.14, communication, planning and resources; Section 3.13, Emergency Operations Centre; Chapters 6–8, Operations, Planning and Logistics; National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction, October 2024, Sections 3.3–3.4 and 4.2; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Chapter XIII, Section 13.3, Emergency Response Infrastructure. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Coordinating Agencies, Communications, Logistics and Mutual Aid
